question: How does hardened oil — hydrogenation, the factory ship, the plantation — turn the world's fats into one industrial system, and where does the fear of fat begin?
summary: Normann's patents of 1902–03 and the first large-scale hardening plant at Warrington in 1906 let liquid oils, whale oil first, become margarine and shortening ([[te1]]). Procter & Gamble follows with Crisco in 1911 ([[te2]], [[e1]]); the margarine makers' raw materials move from coconut to cottonseed to soy ([[ec4]], [[ec5]], [[x1]]); and in 1929 Lever Brothers and the Margarine Union form Unilever ([[ec3]]). Behind them stand the factory ships of the Antarctic — the stern slipway of 1925 and the blue-whale slaughter of 1930–31 — and Lever's purchase of the world's whale oil ([[te3]], [[ec2]], [[ec1]]).

Palm oil is the other half of the supply. Plantations rise in Sumatra from 1911, the Tenera palm is bred, and by 1934 Southeast Asia has overtaken Nigeria ([[ec6]], [[ec10]], [[te4]], [[ec7]]); Lever, refused concessions in West Africa, goes to the Congo ([[ec9]], [[ec8]]). Wars and slumps shape all this: glycerine makes whale oil contraband, the Depression floods the market and Ottawa builds tariff walls, and the Second World War brings rationing and soy margarine ([[c1]], [[w1]], [[o2]], [[c2]]). The Pacific coconut is war material too: glycerine from soap makes copra a strategic crop, and the island plantations change hands after each world war ([[ec11]], [[c1]]).

States tax and then free margarine: the US puts a ten-cent-a-pound tax on yellow margarine in 1902 and repeals it in 1949–50 ([[o1]], [[o4]]); whaling gets a convention in 1931 and the IWC in 1949, and olive oil an international council in 1959 ([[o3]], [[o5]]). And in 1952–61 the fear of dietary fat begins with Keys's hypothesis, Kummerow's early trans-fat warning and the AHA's advice ([[th1]], [[th2]], [[th3]]). Beyond the plantations, Lever’s Nigerian soap works rise from 264 tons in 1924 to over 3,000 in 1929, northern Nigeria’s groundnuts take off when the railway reaches Kano, India’s vanaspati grows from a ghee additive to 43,000 tons in 1941, Lever leases the Solomon Islands for 999 years, and a Unilever survey of Turkey finds a market after Atatürk’s duties ([[ec14]], [[ec15]], [[ec12]], [[ec13]], [[ec16]]). Fish oil, once skimmed from boiled fish for linoleum, paints and soap, grows into the meal-and-oil industry, and the Pacific sardine fishery booms for about twenty years and then collapses ([[ec17]]).

themes.title: Hardening: the technology of one fat becoming another
text: Hydrogenation, Crisco and the shifting mix of margarine fats.

themes.title: Whale oil as an industrial fat
text: Factory ships and Lever's control of the market, regulated only after the slaughter.

themes.title: The palm plantation
text: Hallet, Fauconnier and Lever; the Tenera hybrid; Asia's rise.

themes.title: Margarine and the state
text: From the 1902 tax to its repeal, with wars, tariffs and the Unilever merger in the middle.

themes.title: The fat scare begins
text: Keys, Kummerow and the AHA in the 1950s: a hypothesis, a warning and a recommendation, all contested.

turning_points.text: Normann's hydrogenation patents and the first large hardening plant.
Crisco is launched, the first all-vegetable shortening.
Lever Brothers and the Margarine Union form Unilever.
Southeast Asia overtakes Nigeria in palm oil.
Washington repeals the tax on coloured margarine.
The AHA recommends a low-fat diet.

how_to_read: Read *Technology* first: three machines (hydrogenation, the factory ship, the Tenera palm) reshape three fat chains. *Economy* and *Order* show who gained and who taxed them; *Thought* marks the start of the nutrition fight.
Several tiers are CONTESTED or flagged: Teicholz is a polemical source on the diet–heart story, and van Stuyvenberg's dating of US hardening conflicts with the Crisco date.

The *picture by region* counts the 36 entries: Europe 7, Near East 1, Far East 5, Africa 5, Americas 9, Oceania 2, Worldwide 7. North America and Europe make and regulate fat, Africa and Southeast Asia supply it, and the Pacific supplies copra.

sources.intro: A good documentary base on hardening and margarine (Aoyagi, van Stuyvenberg, Dyer, Fieldhouse, Jones), whaling (Ellis) and palm (Kiple, Zuckerman, Martin, Pye); a journalist's account of the nutrition story.
main: Aoyagi, Hunt in van Stuyvenberg, Dyer et al. and Schleifer ([[te1]], [[te2]], [[e1]]); van Stuyvenberg ([[o1]], [[o4]], [[ec4]], [[e2]]).
Ellis ([[c1]], [[te3]], [[ec1]], [[ec2]], [[o3]]); Jones and Fieldhouse ([[ec3]], [[ec8]]); Kiple, Zuckerman, Pye, Martin ([[ec6]], [[ec7]], [[ec9]], [[ec10]], [[te4]]).
Fieldhouse, *Unilever Overseas*, for India, Nigeria, the Solomon Islands and Turkey ([[ec12]], [[ec14]], [[ec13]], [[ec16]]); Hopkins for the Kano groundnuts ([[ec15]]).
Kiple (O’Keefe) for fish oil and the Pacific sardine fishery ([[ec17]]).
contested: Keys's hypothesis and the AHA's advice ([[th1]], [[th3]]); Kummerow's warning ([[th2]]).
Whether Crisco founded the trans-fat age ([[te2]]); the date hardening reached the US ([[ec4]]).
Kiple's soy account dates a tariff to 1923, which looks wrong, and the folio does not repeat it ([[ec5]]).
gaps: Africa and India in the age of hardening, the German and Japanese fat economies, and olive oil under the Spanish and Italian regimes are missing.
No source for the first hardened butter substitutes in Britain, or for oil-seed crushing in India.
Latin America beyond the United States has no entry; the Near East has one (Turkey in 1939), and Africa beyond Lever’s concessions, Nigerian soap and groundnuts is missing.

text: The makers and sellers: Normann’s hardening patents, Lever’s purchase of the world’s whale oil, Unilever, Blue Band and ‘Nut Lard’, the factory ship from Vestfold, and the International Olive Oil Council ([[te1]], [[ec1]], [[ec3]], [[e2]], [[e3]], [[te3]], [[o5]]).

One entry: Turkey in 1939, where Atatürk’s duties had destroyed the import trade in edible fats and a Unilever survey found a market for margarine and ghee substitute, with a local firm claiming three-quarters of organised oil sales ([[ec16]]).

Southeast Asia overtakes Nigeria in palm oil, with Sumatra and Malaya’s plantations; Manchurian soy goes to Europe; and India’s vanaspati grows from a ghee additive to 43,000 tons a year ([[ec6]], [[ec10]], [[ec7]], [[x1]], [[ec12]]).

Lever is refused West Africa and turns to the Congo; the Tenera palm is bred at Yangambi and in Cameroon ([[ec9]], [[ec8]], [[te4]]); Lever’s soap works at Apapa make Nigeria a manufacturer; and northern Nigeria’s groundnut exports take off with the railway to Kano, on Hausa traders’ initiative ([[ec14]], [[ec15]]). Apart from the groundnut entry these are company histories; African growers appear as labour and as a market.

Crisco and Ivorydale, the colour tax and its repeal, the soy crush at Decatur, margarine’s changing fats and the first diet–heart warnings ([[te2]], [[e1]], [[o1]], [[o4]], [[ec5]], [[ec4]], [[th1]], [[th2]], [[th3]]).

Two entries: the Pacific coconut as glycerine and war material, with the plantations of the Philippines and Indonesia taken in 1942, and Lever’s 999-year lease of the Solomon Islands ([[ec11]], [[ec13]]).

The wars for glycerine and for fats, imperial preference, the whaling convention, the Antarctic slaughter and the glut of the Depression ([[c1]], [[c2]], [[o2]], [[o3]], [[ec2]], [[w1]]). Fish oil and the Pacific sardine fishery add the other marine fat ([[ec17]]).
